_meta.status: NOT PRACTITIONER-REVIEWED. See rubric.md and calibration-plan.md before shipping.
_meta.instrument: Voice-captured open response, graded by the judge against rubric.md. NOT multiple choice.
_meta.schema_note: Eight fields are the engine's existing schema: id, persona, track, prompt, terms, good, bad, model_answer. Two fields are additive extensions the build agent must confirm the loader tolerates: `axes` (required — without it there is no 6-axis scorecard, and the scorecard is the share artifact) and `followups` (the conditional probes that make the counterpart feel like an interviewer rather than a question-reader). Hard numeric constraints are baked into `prompt` text rather than a separate `constraints` field, so the prompt is self-contained and speakable.
design_rules: Every prompt states hard numbers and asks for exactly ONE decision plus its reason. A full 45-minute design cannot be answered in 60 seconds; a single load-bearing judgement call can.
Every model_answer contains at least one concrete number, with its derivation or its assumption stated out loud. A model answer without a number teaches the judge that vagueness scores 20.
Every `bad` is a real failure mode observed in the category, not an invented wrong answer. Several are failure modes the published interview guides name directly.

`terms` is diagnostic vocabulary, NOT a keyword scorer. Presence of a term is not credit; absence of all of them alongside a correct decision is a communication finding, not a knowledge finding. The judge must be instructed accordingly or it degrades into bingo.
Surface is AI infra. Substance is capacity math, queueing, backpressure, multi-tenancy, consistency. Say so on the public pages.

`followups` must ASK, never TELL. A probe that states the insight the candidate was supposed to produce breaks Prompt 1 rule 1, and then the `first_raised_by` clamp penalises the candidate for using a leak the item handed them. Three reviewers independently found three different leading probes; all are rewritten. Escalation branches are labelled `at_bar_1`, `at_bar_2`, never two branches with the same `if`, because Prompt 2 selects a probe verbatim by matching that label and a tie makes the diagnostic non-deterministic — which destroys the percentile.
_meta.sourcing_discipline: No item claims that any named company asks any question. Reported frontier-lab themes (inference batching with explicit capacity math, GPU credit management, low-latency GPU inference with multi-tenancy and cost control) are documented in RESEARCH-NOTES.md as third-party reported, and are used here only to choose which categories to cover. Each item is representative of its category.

personas.inference_lead: Runs the hosted inference fleet. Cares about TTFT, utilisation, and the bill. Pushes on numbers.
personas.platform_staff: Staff engineer on the ML platform. Owns multi-tenancy and quota. Pushes on isolation and blast radius.
personas.research_eng: Research engineer who is the internal customer. Asks for things that are expensive. Pushes on why not.
personas.reliability_eng: On-call for the serving path. Pushes on partial failure, retries, and what the user sees when it breaks.

questions.prompt: We serve a 70-billion-parameter model on replicas of four H100s. Our p99 time-to-first-token target is 400 milliseconds. Right now we use a fixed batch size of 32 with a one-second fill timeout, so a batch departs when it is full or when the timeout expires, whichever comes first. p99 time-to-first-token is sitting at 1.2 seconds, and the GPUs are only 45 percent utilised. Both numbers are bad at the same time. What do you change first, and what number tells you it worked?
questions.good: Identifies that a fixed batch size makes latency depend on batch fill time rather than on work, so requests wait for the batch to fill while GPUs idle — which is exactly how both numbers get bad together. Better: notices that at a one-second fill timeout the batch is departing on the timeout rather than on being full, which is why the system pays the whole wait and still gets a half-empty batch. Strongest: budgets against prefill, not against the decode floor — a 2,000-token prefill is already most of a 400ms target, so the admission window is what prefill leaves over, and quoting the decode floor as the budget is an order-of-magnitude error in the candidate's favour. Moves to continuous batching, where the scheduler admits work per decode step instead of per batch. Sizes the batch *window* against the 400ms budget rather than picking a batch size. Separates prefill from decode scheduling, because a long prefill in the same step blocks every decode behind it. Names the trade-off in units: batch window versus time-to-first-token, or throughput versus tail latency, and picks a side given the stated 400ms. Says what to measure — p99 TTFT and inter-token latency as separate series, not one latency number.
questions.bad: Raises the batch size to improve utilisation. This is the real and common failure: it does raise utilisation and it makes the 1.2 second p99 worse, because with static batching the wait is the batch fill time. The underlying mistake is treating utilisation and latency as one dial. A second common form is 'autoscale the replicas' — which adds idle capacity to a problem caused by scheduling discipline, and does not change the fill time at all.
questions.model_answer: Both numbers are bad together because the batch is departing on the timeout, not on being full: we pay the whole one-second wait and still run half empty. Two quantities say so. 140 gigabytes of weights plus the batch's KV — 32 requests at 2,000 tokens is another 21 — over 13.4 terabytes a second aggregate, so a decode step floors near 12 milliseconds and serves the whole batch. And a 2,000-token prefill is about 0.29 petaflops, roughly 180 milliseconds at realistic utilisation — nearly half the 400 millisecond target before any queueing. So prefill owns the budget, not decode. I would switch to continuous batching and size the admission window against what prefill leaves, 20 to 25 milliseconds, rather than picking a batch size. The trade-off is explicit: a wider window buys throughput and spends tail latency, and at 400 milliseconds I spend throughput. I would watch p99 time-to-first-token and inter-token latency as separate series.

followups.probe: What sets the floor on a decode step here?
Utilisation goes up. What happens to the 1.2 second p99, and why?
You have added two idle replicas and the p99 has not moved. Why not?
Now 30 percent of traffic arrives with 100,000-token prompts. Does your window still hold?
Halve the GPU budget. What breaks first — the 400 milliseconds or the throughput?

questions.prompt: Same 70-billion-parameter model, eight nodes of eight H100s. 95 percent of requests carry about 2,000 tokens of context; 5 percent carry about 100,000. At the daily peak, the long requests push the short ones out of cache and p99 time-to-first-token on the short traffic triples. Before you design anything: what exactly are you protecting, and what is the first number you would want?
questions.good: Refuses to design until the thing being protected is named as a quantity: a time-to-first-token target for the 95 percent, and a separate, explicitly worse one for the long-context 5 percent — two request classes with two SLOs rather than one average. Asks for KV bytes per token, because that is what converts context length into a capacity number, and computes the long request's footprint. Recognises this as a capacity and admission problem, not a cache-tuning problem. States a scope cut out loud: the long-context class gets a worse guarantee on purpose, and says what that buys.
questions.bad: Treats it as an eviction-policy question and starts proposing LRU versus LFU for the KV cache. This is a real and attractive wrong turn — it is a cache, so cache instincts fire — but at these sizes no replacement policy helps, because a single 100,000-token request needs tens of gigabytes that simply are not there alongside the short traffic. The related failure is averaging the two classes into one p99 target, which makes the 5 percent invisible in the metric and the 95 percent unprotectable by policy.
questions.model_answer: What I am protecting is the 95 percent — say a 400 millisecond time-to-first-token target — and I want the long-context class explicitly held to a worse number, maybe two seconds, rather than hidden in a blended p99. The number I want first is KV bytes per token. For a 70B-class model, grouped-query attention with 8 key-value heads, 80 layers, head dimension 128, in bfloat16, that is 2 times 80 times 8 times 128 times 2 bytes, about 320 kilobytes per token. So one 100,000-token request is roughly 32 gigabytes of KV — about 5 percent of a whole 640-gigabyte node, or 41 percent of a single card, on cards each already holding 35 gigabytes of weights. That reframes the problem: this is admission control, not eviction. No replacement policy recovers 32 gigabytes. So I would partition capacity by request class, admit long-context requests against a reserved pool, and shed or queue them when it is full, which makes the degradation land on the class I have already agreed can be slower.

followups.probe: How much KV memory does one of those 100,000-token requests actually need?
How much memory would a policy have to free here? Can any of them free it?
Your p99 is a blend of two classes. What does that metric tell you to do?
Product says long-context is the premium tier and must be fast. Now what?
What do you return to a rejected long-context request, and what does the client do with it?

questions.prompt: A hosted API with 800 tenants. Each is sold 100,000 tokens per minute. Request shapes vary by roughly 100x — some tenants send 500-token requests thousands of times a minute, others send single requests with 100,000 tokens of context. Where does the rate limiter live, and what does it count?
questions.good: Counts tokens, not requests — with 100x shape variance a request limiter provides no isolation at all. Notices that output tokens are not known at admission time, so the limiter must reserve against an estimate and reconcile on completion. Places the check at the gateway for cheap rejection and a second enforcement point at the scheduler, because the gateway cannot know queue depth. Names the trade-off in units: accuracy of the limit versus the latency of the check, or utilisation versus isolation, and picks a side. Observes that one 100,000-token request consumes an entire minute of a tenant's quota in a single call, which makes the limit itself the wrong shape and is worth saying to the product owner.
questions.bad: A requests-per-minute limiter at the gateway. This is the default thing to build and it fails specifically here: it is the limiter nearly every API starts with, and at 100x shape variance it lets one tenant consume orders of magnitude more compute than another while both appear compliant. The second real failure is a strongly consistent central counter in the hot path, which turns every request into a synchronous round trip to one shard and makes the limiter the availability bottleneck for the whole API.
questions.model_answer: It has to count tokens, because requests are not comparable here — 100x shape variance means a request limiter gives you no isolation. 100,000 tokens a minute is about 1,670 tokens a second, so one 100,000-token request spends a tenant's entire minute in a single call. Worth flagging to product: the quota as sold cannot express what a long-context tenant buys. The design follows from that number — a token bucket per tenant, enforced at the gateway so rejection is cheap, with per-node buckets holding leases from a central ledger and reconciling asynchronously. Output length is unknown at admission, so I reserve an estimate and settle on completion. The trade-off is precision against latency: strict global accounting is a synchronous hop per request and a single point of failure, so I take eventual accounting and a bounded few-percent overshoot. I would reverse that the day we sell paid overage, because then those few percent are revenue and the lease has to shrink toward 1,670 tokens. The ledger is what breaks first, so that is what I would load-test.

followups.probe: Tenant A sends 2,000 short requests, tenant B sends 10 long ones. Both are inside the limit. Who is using the fleet?
That shard is now in the path of every request. What is your availability?
You do not know the output length at admission. What do you charge?
One tenant is 40 percent of total traffic and is inside their limit. Is the system fair?
Where is the overshoot bounded, and what is the worst case in dollars?

questions.prompt: An internal GPU credit system. 400 research teams, credits debited per GPU-second, and 20 schedulers admitting jobs. Jobs must start in under 2 seconds. A strongly consistent ledger check adds about 150 milliseconds to admission, and puts the ledger in the path of every job start. What consistency model do you pick, and what is the exposure if you are wrong?
questions.good: Picks leases: each scheduler draws a block of credits ahead of time and debits locally, so the ledger leaves the admission path entirely. States what the bound is conditional on: the lease bound holds only while the ledger is reachable, and exposure during an outage turns on whether admission fails open or closed — two orders of magnitude apart. Quantifies the exposure as the bound on overdraft — lease size times scheduler count — and converts it to dollars, which is what makes the choice obviously correct rather than merely fashionable. Names the real risk as the availability coupling, not the 150 milliseconds: a linearizable ledger in the path means no job in the company starts when that ledger is degraded. Says what happens on scheduler death (the lease is lost or reclaimed on a timer) and makes debits idempotent so reconciliation cannot double-charge.
questions.bad: Chooses strong consistency because credits are money and money needs transactions. This is a genuinely defensible-sounding answer and it is the common one, which is why it discriminates: it accepts a hard availability coupling for every job start across the company in exchange for preventing an overdraft that is worth a few dollars. The failure is not the consistency choice, it is never having sized the thing being protected. The opposite real failure is choosing eventual consistency without bounding the overdraft at all, which is the same mistake with a different outcome.
questions.model_answer: I would take leases and keep the ledger out of the admission path. Each of the 20 schedulers holds a lease of, say, 1,000 GPU-seconds, debits locally, and reconciles asynchronously. Worst-case overdraft is then computable: 20 times 1,000 is 20,000 GPU-seconds, 5.6 GPU-hours, about 11 dollars at 2 dollars an hour. But 11 dollars only bounds it while leases hold. If the ledger is unreachable and I fail open, the exposure is the whole fleet burning un-debited — 2,000 GPUs through a ten-minute outage is about 333 GPU-hours, roughly 670 dollars, and still accruing. So I fail closed: a scheduler that cannot renew stops admitting. So I trade 11 dollars of overspend for removing a hard dependency from every job start — and that dependency is the real exposure, not the 150 milliseconds: a linearizable ledger in the path means nobody's research runs when it degrades. At 11,000 dollars instead of 11 I would shrink the lease, not change the model. Debits need idempotency keys, and leases a timeout so a dead scheduler's credits return.

followups.probe: Put a number on what you are protecting. What is the exposure worth?
How far negative can a team go before you notice?
A scheduler dies holding a lease. Where did those credits go?
Finance wants a per-team invoice that reconciles to the cent. Does your design survive that?
What is the first signal that reconciliation is silently wrong?

questions.prompt: 60,000 concurrent streaming sessions. A typical answer streams for about 90 seconds. Mobile clients drop their connection at roughly 4 percent per minute. We deploy about six times a day. Pick your transport, and tell me what happens to an in-flight stream when a node goes away mid-generation.
questions.good: Picks SSE for a one-directional token stream and gives a reason tied to this system (simpler, works over plain HTTP, reconnection semantics are built in) rather than a general preference. Does the reconnection arithmetic: at 4 percent per minute over a 90-second answer, a meaningful fraction of streams break, so resumption is a core requirement rather than an edge case. Designs resumption explicitly — a token index or cursor the client sends back, with generated tokens buffered server-side so a reconnect resumes rather than restarts. Addresses deploys as the same failure, not a separate one: connection draining, and generation state that outlives the process holding the socket. Names what the user sees in the unrecoverable case.
questions.bad: Picks WebSocket for bidirectional capability it does not need, then adds sticky sessions to make it work — which couples every in-flight stream to one process and makes six deploys a day into six waves of broken streams. The deeper and more common failure is treating reconnection as a client retry that restarts generation: the user pays twice, waits twice, and on a side-effecting or billed path is charged twice. Not buffering generated tokens server-side is the specific omission that forces this.
questions.model_answer: Server-sent events. The stream is one-directional, it is plain HTTP so proxies and mobile networks handle it, and reconnection is part of the protocol. The arithmetic forces the real design: 4 percent a minute over a 90-second answer means roughly 6 percent of streams break mid-generation, which at 60,000 concurrent is thousands of resumptions at any moment. So resumption is the feature, not an edge case. I buffer generated tokens server-side against a stream ID and have the client reconnect with the index of the last token it saw, so it resumes instead of regenerating — otherwise the user waits twice and, on a billed path, pays twice. Deploys are the same failure at larger scale: six a day means generation state cannot live in the process holding the socket, so I keep it in the inference service with the socket as a thin reader, and drain connections rather than cutting them. If the buffer has expired, the client gets an explicit restart signal rather than silence.

followups.probe: What do you need the upstream channel for in a token stream?
You deploy six times a day. What happens to the sticky sessions?
The user has seen 400 tokens and reconnects. Do they see them again, and who pays for them?
How long do you hold the buffer, and what does that cost at 60,000 concurrent?
The client is a server-side integration, not a browser. Does anything change?

questions.prompt: Policy says a safety classifier runs on every request. It costs 40 milliseconds at p50 and 180 at p99. Our time-to-first-token budget is 400 milliseconds and we are already at 310 at p99. Your tech lead proposes running it asynchronously alongside generation and killing the stream at the first unsafe token. What do you say to them?
questions.good: Engages the actual proposal rather than restating policy, and credits the part that is right: killing the stream is a genuine mitigation. Handles the arithmetic correctly — does NOT add the two p99 figures, because the p99 of a sum is not the sum of p99s, while still concluding that 90 milliseconds of headroom cannot absorb a stage whose own p99 is 180, so the current shape fails either way. Names what async actually costs: tokens already rendered before the kill, which is a policy decision with an owner rather than an engineering tradeoff. Proposes a third option — classify the prompt during prefill so the cost overlaps work already being done — and gates only the first output flush. Escalates the fail-open versus fail-closed call rather than deciding it. Keeps the register collaborative.
questions.bad: Wins on policy — 'we have to, it is required' — without addressing that the budget does not close either way. Technically right, heard as inflexible, and leaves the room with no design. The arithmetic failure that looks like rigour is adding the two p99s to get 490 and presenting that as the combined tail: p99s do not add, and a reviewer who knows that stops trusting the rest of the answer. The third real failure is accepting async without ever naming that someone is now choosing to let unsafe output render, which is not the tech lead's call to make alone.
questions.model_answer: First, their proposal is coherent — killing the stream is a real mitigation, not a hand-wave. Two things give me pause. One is arithmetic: I cannot just add 310 and 180, because the p99 of a sum is not the sum of the p99s. But I do not need to — with 90 milliseconds of headroom and a stage whose own p99 is 180, the tail does not fit however I compose them. So we agree the current shape is wrong. Two is what async buys. Killing at the first unsafe token means some unsafe tokens already rendered on someone's screen. That may be acceptable, but it is a policy call with a named owner, not ours to make here. What I would propose instead is classifying the prompt during prefill — for a 2,000-token prompt that is already hundreds of milliseconds we are paying for, so most of the 40 milliseconds overlaps and costs almost nothing. For output we gate the first flush only.

followups.probe: I agree it is required. The budget still does not close. What is your design?
Walk me through that addition again. Is the p99 of a sum the sum of the p99s?
How many tokens render before the kill lands, and who signed off on that?
How much headroom do we have, and how much does the classifier want?
The classifier is down. Do you serve or refuse, and who decides?
Prompt classification is clean but the output turns unsafe at token 500. What did your design buy?

questions.prompt: Three models in production: 8 billion, 70 billion, and 400 billion parameters, on a mixed fleet of A100s and H100s. We are at two dollars sixty per million output tokens today, everything on the 70B, and finance has given you a blended ceiling of one dollar fifty. Offline evaluation says about 70 percent of current traffic would be served acceptably by the 8-billion model; a few percent genuinely needs the 400B. How do you route, and what do you measure to know you have not quietly made the product worse?
questions.good: Derives the cost ratio from first principles — decode cost tracks weight bytes read, so the 8B is roughly an order of magnitude cheaper per token than the 70B and the 400B several times more expensive. Computes the blend against the stated $2.60 baseline rather than against an unstated one, so the comparison to the $1.50 ceiling is actually derivable. The discriminating move is noticing that the small share on the largest model dominates the bill: a few percent on the 400B outweighs the whole 70 percent saving on the 8B, so the binding lever is the 400B escalation rate, not the 8B share, and the threshold that follows is a 400B share under roughly 4 percent. Treats escalation rate as the cost control. On measurement, tracks quality per traffic segment and escalation rate rather than aggregate quality, because a partly-wrong router holds the average flat while destroying one segment. Proposes shadow traffic before a cutover.
questions.bad: Routes on prompt length or another cheap proxy for difficulty and measures aggregate quality. Both halves are real: length is the proxy everyone reaches for and it correlates weakly with the difficulty of the response, and aggregate quality is the metric that hides the damage, because the misrouted minority is averaged against the majority that was fine. The specific arithmetic failure is optimising the 8B share while ignoring the 400B's: with a 5x cost multiplier, a few percent of traffic on the largest model can exceed the entire saving from the small one, so a candidate who only tunes the 70 percent never reaches the ceiling.
questions.model_answer: Cost per token roughly tracks weight bytes read, so relative to the 70B the 8B is about a tenth and the 400B five to six times more. Baseline is two sixty. Send 70 percent to the 8B, 25 to the 70B and 5 to the 400B: the blend is 0.7 times 0.1, plus 0.25, plus 0.05 times 5.7 — about 0.6 of baseline, so roughly one fifty-seven. Over the ceiling, and the interesting part is why: the 5 percent on the 400B costs four times what the whole 70 percent on the 8B saves. So the lever is the 400B's share, not the small model — I need it under about 4 percent. I would route with a cheap classifier, cascade on low confidence, and treat the 400B escalation rate as the cost dial. Measure quality per traffic segment and escalation rate, not aggregate quality, because a router that is 70 percent right holds the average flat while wrecking one segment.

followups.probe: What is the blended cost per million tokens under your routing? Is it under the ceiling?
A 30-token prompt asks for a proof. A 3,000-token prompt asks for a summary. Which model does each get?
Average quality is flat and support tickets are up 40 percent. What happened?
The router itself adds 30 milliseconds. Where does that come from in the budget?
Finance halves the ceiling. What do you change — the split, the models, or the product?

questions.prompt: I am a research engineer and I want 50,000 graded evaluations on every commit. We land about 40 commits a day. Each evaluation is one 2,000-token generation plus a judge call. I want results in under 10 minutes so it can gate merges. Tell me what that costs, and tell me what you would push back on.
questions.good: Produces the capacity number before the opinion, because the number is the argument: 50,000 evaluations times 2,000 tokens in 600 seconds is a sustained token rate that implies a specific fleet size, and that fleet size times 40 commits a day is a specific daily bill. Then pushes back on the requirement rather than the implementation: the 10-minute gate on every commit is the expensive clause, and it is the one that was never costed. Offers the cheaper shapes — sample on commit and run the full suite on merge, cache results keyed by anything the commit did not change, shard and early-abort on a decisive subset. Treats the researcher as a customer whose goal is real: asks what decision the gate is meant to make, because a flake-prone gate blocking 40 merges a day is worse than no gate. Keeps the register collaborative rather than obstructive.
questions.bad: Says yes and builds it, or says no on cost without ever producing the number. Both are real and both are communication failures more than engineering ones. The specific technical failure under the 'yes' is not asking about the flake rate: at 50,000 evaluations per commit, even a very small nondeterministic failure rate means the gate blocks merges constantly, the team learns to override it, and the expensive infrastructure is then load-bearing for nothing.
questions.model_answer: Let me cost it before I argue with it. 50,000 evaluations at 2,000 tokens in 600 seconds is about 170,000 tokens a second. A four-H100 replica serving a 70B does about 4,700 tokens a second once KV reads are counted, so roughly 35 replicas, 141 GPUs, for ten minutes a commit, plus judge calls. At 2 dollars a GPU-hour that is about 47 dollars a commit, 1,900 a day, roughly 690,000 a year — and that assumes I can rent 141 H100s ten minutes at a time. Reserved for a 28 percent duty cycle it is nearer 2.5 million, so the elasticity assumption matters more than the arithmetic. What I would push back on is not the 50,000, it is 'every commit, gating merges, in 10 minutes', which is nearly all of the cost. Sample a few thousand on commit, full suite on merge, cache by content hash. And what is your flake rate?

followups.probe: I need a figure to take to my lead. What is it?

followups.if: refuses on cost without a number
followups.probe: You may be right, but I cannot act on 'expensive'. What is the figure?
What is our flake rate, and what happens to the merge queue when the gate trips?
I will take sampling on commit. How do you pick the sample so it is not useless?
Who gets billed for this, and can you attribute it per team?

questions.prompt: Our preference-data pipeline produces 200,000 human comparisons a month with 120 annotators. Inter-annotator agreement is a Cohen's kappa of 0.62. A VP asks why we cannot just double the annotator pool and get 400,000. You have about 30 seconds and they are not an ML person.
questions.good: Answers in the VP's units — months, money, whether the model improves — not in ML vocabulary. Crucially, does NOT claim that agreement work beats volume on effective sample size: doubling the pool does roughly double usable data, and a candidate who denies that is wrong. The correct argument is about sequencing and compounding: a kappa improvement raises the value of every comparison collected afterwards, including the doubled pool's, so doing agreement first and volume second strictly dominates the reverse order. Names the second-order cost — 120 unramped annotators dilute agreement before they add throughput. Gives a timeline and commits to returning with a number.
questions.bad: Explains Cohen's kappa to the VP. Accurate, responsive, and loses the room, which on this axis is the whole measurement. The substantive failure is the one that sounds sophisticated: arguing that raising agreement is worth MORE than doubling volume. It is not, on effective sample size — lifting kappa from 0.62 to 0.80 buys about 1.3x while doubling the pool buys 2x. A candidate who makes the stronger claim is both wrong and checkable, and a VP who later checks it stops trusting the next estimate.
questions.model_answer: You are right that doubling the pool roughly doubles the usable data — I do not want to pretend otherwise. My argument is about order. At a kappa of 0.62, a meaningful slice of every comparison we buy is closer to a coin flip than a signal, so we are paying for 200,000 a month and banking materially less. That waste applies to everything we collect from here on. Six weeks of tightening the guidelines and adjudicating against a gold set lifts the value of every future comparison by roughly a quarter to a third — including all 400,000 a month from the bigger pool. Do it the other way round and we pay twice for the same noise, and it is worse than that short-term, because 120 unramped annotators pull agreement down further before they lift throughput. So: six weeks on agreement, then double the pool, and I will come back and ask for the headcount with a number attached.

followups.probe: I do not know what that is. Tell me in terms of whether the model gets better.
We doubled it and the model did not move. What do I tell my boss?
How long does your alternative take, and what do I get at the end?
What agreement number would make you comfortable scaling?
Could a model do the first pass and humans only adjudicate? What breaks?

questions.prompt: A 4-petabyte raw text corpus that tokenises to about 80 terabytes. It needs deduplication and a global shuffle, 2,000 GPUs will read it during training, and a run has to be reproducible down to the exact batch six months later. The dedup job currently takes nine days and nobody trusts the shuffle. What breaks first, and what do you fix first?
questions.good: Separates the three requirements, because they fail for different reasons and one is cheap: reproducibility is a manifest-and-seed problem, not a data-processing one, fixable in days. Distinguishes the raw corpus from the tokenised one before costing the shuffle — three orders of magnitude apart, and only one is on the training path. Treats the shuffle as an I/O budget and gets the budget right — a global shuffle READS and WRITES the corpus, so 4PB of data is 8PB of movement. Distinguishes corpus-scale I/O from the bandwidth the GPUs actually need to stay fed, which is orders of magnitude smaller because tokens are small; the binding term on the training read path is access pattern and IOPS, not bytes per second. Names the trust problem as a missing measurement rather than a worse algorithm. Leaves dedup last because it runs once per corpus version.
questions.bad: Optimises the nine-day dedup job first, because it is the biggest visible number. It is the wrong first move: dedup runs once per corpus version, nine days is survivable, and meanwhile the untrusted shuffle and the missing reproducibility are silently contaminating every run and every comparison between runs. The specific technical failure is implementing the shuffle as a per-epoch global operation, which quietly requires moving petabytes every epoch and is the usual reason a data pipeline cannot keep 2,000 GPUs fed.
questions.model_answer: Three requirements, three failure modes, and the nine days is the least urgent. Reproducibility is cheapest: content-address the shards, then record the manifest, the seed and the ordering function with the run — that regenerates the exact batch sequence six months later without storing it. Second, the shuffle, and which corpus. The raw 4 petabytes reads 4 and writes 4, so it moves 8 — 22 hours at 100 gigabytes a second. The 80-terabyte tokenised corpus moves 160, about 27 minutes, cheap enough to run every epoch. The petabyte figure constrains nothing, and it is not what keeps 2,000 GPUs fed either — tokens are tiny, so that is an IOPS problem. Then the failure mode in what I just proposed: if shards are built in crawl order, in-shard shuffling gives the same neighbourhoods every epoch, so batches stay correlated and the loss curve looks healthy while the model sees less diversity than we think. So randomise shard assignment at ingest too, and watch batch token distribution against a held-out sample. Dedup stays at nine days, off the critical path.

followups.probe: What is the cadence of each of those three jobs?
How many bytes does that move per epoch, and how long does it take?
How much storage is that for a run, and for the 40 runs you compare?
A shard is found to be corrupt three months after the run. What can you say about the run?
2,000 GPUs are at 60 percent utilisation waiting on data. Where is the bottleneck?

questions.prompt: Retrieval over 10 billion embeddings at 1,024 dimensions, stored as float32. The p99 budget for the retrieval step is 50 milliseconds, recall at 10 must stay at or above 0.9, and about 200 million vectors change every day. Pick an index and tell me what the choice costs you.
questions.good: Starts with the memory number, because it eliminates most of the option space immediately: 10 billion times 1,024 times 4 bytes is tens of terabytes, which cannot sit in RAM at any sane cost, so the choice is really about what to compress and what to recover. Picks a quantized index — product quantization over an inverted-file structure — computes the compressed footprint, and shows it now fits across a modest cluster. Names the trade-off in units rather than in adjectives: compression ratio against recall, and recovers the lost recall with a reranking pass over full-precision vectors for the top candidates, which spends part of the 50 millisecond budget on purpose. Handles the 2 percent daily churn as an architectural requirement, not an afterthought: incremental additions into a small live segment plus periodic merges, because a full rebuild at this size cannot keep a daily cadence.
questions.bad: Picks HNSW because it has the best recall-latency curve in the benchmarks. This is the most defensible-looking wrong answer in the set and it is a real mistake: HNSW's graph plus full-precision vectors at this scale needs tens of terabytes of RAM, and it handles high deletion and update churn poorly, so the 200 million daily changes degrade it. The second real failure is quantizing hard enough to fit, never measuring recall at 10, and discovering in production that retrieval quality fell below the 0.9 floor — the number was in the requirements and never checked.
questions.model_answer: The memory number decides this. 10 billion vectors at 1,024 dimensions in float32 is about 40 terabytes raw, so nothing that needs full-precision vectors resident is affordable — that rules out a plain HNSW graph, which would also suffer with 200 million changes a day. So: an inverted-file index with product quantization. At roughly 64 bytes a vector after quantization that is about 640 gigabytes, which fits across ten or so machines with room for the coarse centroids. The cost is recall: aggressive quantization loses exactly the thing the 0.9 floor protects. So I spend part of the budget buying it back — retrieve a few hundred candidates from the compressed index, then rerank them against full-precision vectors fetched from disk or a cache, which is a small enough set to afford inside 50 milliseconds. For the churn, 200 million a day is about 2 percent, so I would write new vectors into a small live segment searched alongside the main index and merge periodically, because a full rebuild cannot run daily at this size.

followups.probe: How much memory does the raw set need? Does your index fit on one machine?
What is the resident memory for that graph at 10 billion vectors, and what do 200 million daily deletions do to it?
You compressed 60-fold. What is recall at 10 now, and how do you know?
A full rebuild takes 30 hours and you have daily churn. What is your freshness guarantee?
Halve the machine budget. Do you give up recall or latency?

questions.prompt: An agent fans out to 12 tools per turn. Some have side effects — one sends email, one charges a card. p99 tool latency is 8 seconds and each tool times out about 2 percent of the time. Today, when any tool times out, the orchestrator retries the whole turn. A teammate's fix is to add retries at the tool layer instead. Where is the actual bug, and what do you say to them?
questions.good: Computes the compound failure probability, which is the move that reframes the whole conversation: with 12 tools at 2 percent each, something times out on roughly a fifth of all turns — stated as the upper bound it is, since independence is an assumption and a shared deadline correlates the failures, so this is the normal path, not an edge case. Locates the bug correctly: retrying the whole turn re-executes side effects, so at that rate a meaningful share of turns send duplicate email or double-charge — and that is a correctness bug, not a reliability one. Says why tool-layer retries do not fix it and partly make it worse: a timeout does not tell you whether the call completed, so retrying a charge without an idempotency key charges twice, and retries at two layers multiply. The fix is idempotency keys per logical operation plus a timeout budget, with retries only on operations that are safe or made safe. Handles the teammate's proposal by crediting the part that is right (whole-turn retry is wrong) before disagreeing on the fix.
questions.bad: Adds retries at the tool layer, which is the teammate's proposal and is genuinely tempting because it is more targeted than retrying the turn. It does not address that a timed-out charge may have succeeded, so the retry double-charges, and retries at both the tool and orchestrator layers multiply into retry amplification against a dependency that is probably already slow for a reason. The other real failure is treating a 2 percent per-tool timeout rate as rare and not multiplying it by 12.
questions.model_answer: Multiply it out first: 12 tools at 2 percent each is about 21 percent of turns, and that is an upper bound — it assumes independence, and a shared turn-level deadline correlates the failures downward. So whole-turn retry is not a rare path, it is the normal path, and the actual bug is that it re-executes side effects. At that rate we are duplicating emails and double-charging cards routinely. That is a correctness bug, not a reliability one. My teammate is right that whole-turn retry has to go, but tool-layer retries miss the problem: a timeout tells you nothing about whether the call completed, so retrying a charge just charges again. What I want is an idempotency key per logical operation, generated once per turn, so a retry at any layer is a no-op if the first attempt landed. Then a shared timeout budget across the fan-out, retries only on read-only or idempotent calls, and a compensating action for the ones we cannot make idempotent.

followups.probe: How often does at least one of the 12 time out? Work it through.
The charge call timed out. Did it charge? What does your retry do?

followups.if: treats it as a rare edge case
followups.probe: Is this a rare path or a common one? What decides that?
The email provider has no idempotency support. Now what?
How would you have caught this in production before finance did?
